prompt: In `hand.go`, `main` reads two values with `<-results` and has no `WaitGroup`. What stops it from printing before the goroutines have finished?
hint: What does a receive do when no value has been sent yet?

choices.text: Each receive waits until a value has been sent
choices.why: Right. The value arriving is itself the proof that the goroutine got that far.

choices.text: The `time.Sleep` inside `sum` holds `main` back as well
choices.why: A sleep blocks only the goroutine that calls it. `main` is held by its receive.

choices.text: Nothing: it may print before them, and did in one run
choices.why: It cannot print a total before receiving it, and it cannot receive before a send.

choices.text: `make(chan int)` makes `main` the last goroutine to run
choices.why: Making a channel decides nothing about order. Receiving from it does.

prompt: Both totals of `hand.go` arrived at about 200 ms, though each goroutine slept 200 ms. Why not 200 ms and then 400 ms?
hint: Look at the figure in section 02.

choices.text: The channel holds both values, so the second send did not wait
choices.why: `make(chan int)` has no room for values at all; each send waited for a receive.

choices.text: The two goroutines slept at the same time
choices.why: Right. Their waits overlapped, and each send only waited for `main` to be ready.

choices.text: The second goroutine skipped its sleep because the first had slept
choices.why: Each goroutine runs its own copy of `sum`, sleep included.

choices.text: Rounding to 10 ms hid the difference
choices.why: A 200 ms difference would survive rounding to 10 ms easily.

prompt: A colleague needs to know which list each total in `hand.go` came from. In one run the first value received was 60. What should they change?
hint: Which goroutine finishes first is not promised.

choices.text: Start the goroutines in the order the totals are wanted
choices.why: That is what the program already does, and 60 still came first.

choices.text: Add a short sleep between the two `go` statements
choices.why: A sleep makes one order likely on one machine. It promises nothing.

choices.text: Send the list's name along with its total
choices.why: Right. If the value says where it came from, the order it arrives in no longer matters.

choices.text: Use two receives on two separate lines
choices.why: It already does, and both read from one shared channel, which carries no origin.

prompt: A channel declared with `var ch chan int` and never made has the zero value ___.
hint: The same zero value as a map or a pointer.

prompt: `closed.go` sent two strings, closed the channel and received four times. What did the third receive return?
hint: The channel was closed and empty by then.

choices.text: `"second"` again, the last value sent
choices.why: A closed channel does not repeat its last value. It answers with the zero value.

choices.text: It blocked until the program ended
choices.why: Receiving from a closed, empty channel never blocks; that is what close is for.

choices.text: `""` and `false`
choices.why: Right: the element type's zero value, and `ok` false to say the channel is closed.

choices.text: A panic: receive from closed channel
choices.why: Receiving after close is allowed and answers at once. Sending after close is what panics.

prompt: Match each operation on a closed channel with what it does.

pairs.right: the zero value and `false`, at once

prompt: Why does the lesson say only the sending side should close a channel?
hint: What can a receiver not know about the senders?

choices.text: Closing from the receiving side is a compile error
choices.why: Only when the receiver holds a `<-chan` type. With a plain `chan` it compiles, and that is the danger.

choices.text: Nobody else can be sure the sending is over
choices.why: Right. The goroutine that owns the sending is the one that knows it has finished.

choices.text: Closing discards the values still in the channel
choices.why: It does not: `closed.go` received both values sent before the close.

choices.text: A receiver may check whether the channel is closed first
choices.why: There is no such check, and an answer could be out of date by the time it arrived.

prompt: `func drain(in <-chan int)` contains `in <- 1`. When is the mistake found?

choices.text: When `drain` runs, as a panic
choices.why: It never gets that far. A direction is part of the type.

choices.text: Only by the race detector, with `-race`
choices.why: This is not a race; it is a type error.

choices.text: Never: the direction is a comment for readers
choices.why: The compiler enforces it, and refused `oops.go`.

choices.text: At compile time: cannot send to receive-only channel
choices.why: Right. `go build` refused before anything ran, naming the type `<-chan int`.

prompt: What ends `for w := range words` in `words.go`?
hint: Delete one line and the loop never ends.

choices.text: Receiving as many values as `strings.Fields` returned
choices.why: `main` does not know how many words there are; that is why it ranges.

choices.text: `split` closing the channel after the last word
choices.why: Right. The loop receives until the channel is closed and empty.

choices.text: `split` returning
choices.why: In `forgot.go`, `split` returned and the loop waited on.

choices.text: A receive that waits longer than a second
choices.why: A range has no timeout of its own. Lesson 5 adds timeouts with `select`.

prompt: `forgot.go` printed all four words and then `fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!`. What told the runtime the program was stuck?

choices.text: The channel had been open too long
choices.why: The runtime has no notion of a channel being open too long.

choices.text: `main` had received more values than were sent
choices.why: It received exactly the four that were sent, then waited for a fifth.

choices.text: Every goroutine in the program was blocked
choices.why: Right. `split` had returned and `main` waited on a receive, so nothing could ever move.

choices.text: The compiler marked the missing `close`
choices.why: It compiled without complaint. The error came at run time.

prompt: The same forgotten `close` sits in a server, where other goroutines are waiting for connections. What does the student see?
hint: When does the runtime's deadlock check fire?

choices.text: The same fatal error, as soon as the words run out
choices.why: The check fires only when every goroutine is blocked, and the server's are alive.

choices.text: Nothing: the ranging goroutine waits forever, silently
choices.why: Right. That is a goroutine leak, lesson 6's subject.

choices.text: A panic: receive on a channel nobody sends to
choices.why: No such panic exists. Waiting is legal.

choices.text: The loop ends after a timeout the runtime adds
choices.why: The runtime adds no timeouts to channel operations.

prompt: Put the events of `words.go` in order.
hint: A close never overtakes values already sent.
items: the range ends and `main` prints its last line

prompt: `words.go` printed `13 communicating`. How many words did the loop receive in all?
Which of these does a channel do in `hand.go`? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think about the value and about the timing.

choices.text: Carries each goroutine's total to `main`
choices.why: Yes. It replaces the return value the `go` statement throws away.

choices.text: Makes `main` wait until each total exists
choices.why: Yes. A receive cannot finish before a send.

choices.text: Puts the totals in the order the goroutines started
choices.why: 60 arrived first, from the second goroutine started.

choices.text: Copies the slices so the goroutines cannot share them
choices.why: The slices are arguments, copied (as headers) by the call, not by the channel.

prompt: Three goroutines send results on one channel and `main` ranges over it. Which goroutine should close the channel?
hint: Closing early panics the others; closing never hangs `main`.

choices.text: Whichever of the three finishes first
choices.why: The other two may still send, and a send after close panics.

choices.text: `main`, as soon as it has received its first value from them
choices.why: A receiver cannot know the senders are done, and closing under them panics.

choices.text: One that waits until all three are done, then closes
choices.why: Right. None of the three can close alone; lesson 14 builds that waiting goroutine.

choices.text: Each of the three, after its own last send
choices.why: The second close would panic: close of closed channel.

prompt: `main` makes `ch := make(chan int)` and calls `produce(ch)`, where `func produce(out chan<- int)`. What happens to the type?
hint: A plain channel converts to either direction.

choices.text: A compile error: `chan int` is not `chan<- int`
choices.why: The conversion from a two-way channel to one direction is implicit.

choices.text: Inside `produce` it is send-only; `main` keeps both directions
choices.why: Right. Same channel, two views of it: that is how `words.go` gives `split` only the half it needs.

choices.text: A copy of the channel is made for `produce`
choices.why: A channel is a reference; both names point at the one channel.

choices.text: `main` loses the right to receive from `ch`
choices.why: `main`'s variable keeps its own type, `chan int`.

prompt: The loop that receives until a channel is closed and empty is written `for v := ___ ch`.
hint: The same keyword that walks a slice.

prompt: `go run sendclosed.go` panicked. With what exit status did the program end, by the line `go run` printed?
